lines: Jamie Alvarez
+1 (555) 010-5820 | jamie.alvarez@example.com | example.com/in/jalvarez
EDUCATION
Riverbend Polytechnic | B.S. in Industrial Engineering | Metro City, USA | Sep 2014 - May 2018
EXPERIENCE
Greenleaf Florist | Delivery Driver and Shop Assistant | Metro City, USA | Sep 2025 - Present
- Delivered 30 to 40 arrangements a day across the city and took cash and card payments at the door.
- Prepared weekend wedding orders with the head florist and kept the cooler stocked and labeled.
Lakeview Distribution | Operations Analyst | Metro City, USA | Jul 2018 - Jan 2021
- Owned the pick-path layouts for the fast-moving zone and the labor reports the shift leads used.
- Ran a time study of the returns desk; the findings led to a triage station that cut returns processing time from 3 days to 1.
- Wrote the dock scheduling rules for 12 carriers, cutting average trailer wait at the dock from 95 to 40 minutes.

- Set up cycle counting for the 2,000 highest-value locations while also covering night-shift supervision, updating the safety training slides, coordinating holiday temp hiring and running the forklift certification schedule, which raised inventory record accuracy from 91% to 98.5%.
Crestway Foods | Supply Chain Planner | Metro City, USA | Feb 2021 - Jul 2025
- Rebuilt weekly demand planning for 1,400 SKUs across 3 distribution centers with a seasonal forecast model, cutting stockouts from 6.2% to 2.8% while inventory fell by $1.9M.
- Reduced freight costs by 15% by consolidating supplier pickups into regional milk runs.
- Set reorder points for every SKU from 18 months of daily demand and supplier lead-time data, reviewed monthly with the category managers.
- Built the weekly supplier scorecard for 40 vendors, which buyers used to renegotiate delivery windows with the five least reliable.
- Raised the packaging line's overall equipment effectiveness (OEE) from 71% to 112% by cutting changeover time and micro-stops.
- Cut average order lead time through the warehouse from 10 days to 5 while holding daily throughput constant and doubling work-in-process to keep pickers busy.
PROJECTS
Last-Mile Routing Study | Independent Project | Python | Oct 2024 - Present
- Modeled a regional grocer's 85 daily delivery stops as a vehicle-routing problem, cutting planned route miles 18% against the grocer's current routes.
- Checked the planned routes against 4 weeks of real delivery logs; planned drive times came within 5% of the actual ones.
- Shared the model and a one-page summary with the grocer's dispatch team, who piloted the routes on two trucks for a month.
Regional Food Bank Warehouse | Volunteer Consultant, Team of 4 | Excel | Mar 2022 - Jul 2022
- Analyzed warehouse operations and made recommendations to the food bank's leadership.
- The donation intake process was mapped and two duplicate data-entry steps were removed, so donations reached the shelves a day sooner.
- Built a seasonal forecast for 1,400 products across three warehouses that more than halved stockouts and cut inventory by nearly $2M.
SKILLS
Tools: Excel, Python
Methods: demand forecasting, inventory planning, time studies, vehicle routing

items.says: Education leads the résumé even though the established work history is the stronger introduction.
items.because: A reader reaches the degree before the operational results in Experience.

items.says: The experience order puts Lakeview before Crestway and both relevant roles below Greenleaf.
items.because: It obscures the analyst-to-planner progression and puts the less relevant present role first.

items.says: The change from Supply Chain Planner to Delivery Driver and Shop Assistant has no explanation.
items.because: A reader may wonder whether it reflects a deliberate transition, interim work, or a change in target role.

items.says: The delivery count does not show how reliably arrangements arrived on schedule.
The verbs are in past tense although the role is marked Present.
The wedding-order work does not identify the preparation step handled.
The verbs are in past tense although the role is marked Present.
The cooler task does not say what it helped accomplish.
The layout and reporting responsibilities do not say what either improved.
items.because: A reader can see the remit but cannot tell what it was worth operationally.

items.says: “Owned” describes responsibility rather than what was done to the pick-path layouts.
The dock-scheduling result is buried below a less outcome-focused opening bullet.
The dock-scheduling line omits the scheduling decision embodied in the rules.
items.because: A reader cannot tell what scheduling judgment produced the reduction from 95 to 40 minutes.

items.says: Unrelated duties separate cycle counting from its inventory-accuracy result.
items.because: A scanning reader may miss the rise from 91% to 98.5% or attribute it to the intervening duties.

items.says: The reorder-point bullet does not say what changed because of the new thresholds.
items.because: The 18 months of data establishes the basis for the work, not its effect.

items.says: The monthly-review phrase appears to modify the data rather than the reorder points.
items.because: A reader may have to reread the sentence to work out what was reviewed.

items.says: The scorecard bullet does not say what the new delivery windows achieved.
The scorecard does not show how the five least reliable vendors were identified.
The stated OEE of 112% is impossible under the standard OEE definition.
items.because: OEE is availability × performance × quality, with each factor capped at 100%.

items.says: The OEE bullet names losses that fell but not the process change made.
Halving lead time at constant throughput conflicts with the claim that work-in-process doubled.
items.because: For a stable process across the same boundaries, Little’s Law says work-in-process would halve, not double.

items.says: The lead-time bullet does not say what changed in the order flow.
“To keep pickers busy” gives a motive rather than a result.
The comparison to the grocer’s current routes is awkwardly phrased.
The routing bullet does not show how the improved routes were generated.
items.because: A reader cannot assess the modeling work that produced them.

items.says: The 5% difference does not identify the unit or calculation behind it.
“Real” adds nothing to the description of the delivery logs.
The pilot bullet says the routes were tried but not what happened during the pilot.
The broad opening delays specific contributions and omits the analysis’s evidence and the recommendations’ outcome.
items.because: It starts the entry with its least assessable claim beside the more specific bullets that follow.

items.says: The passive wording hides who mapped the intake process and removed the duplicate steps.
The one-day result comes after the process description.
items.because: It is easier to miss there.

items.says: The food-bank forecast repeats the distinctive scope and results credited to Crestway, making the achievement appear misassigned.
items.because: The matching scope and nearly identical results make a reader doubt which organization achieved them.

items.says: “Built a seasonal forecast” does not show how seasonality entered the forecast.
items.because: The method is hard to assess independently of the reported result.

items.says: The forecast claim appears below the generic opening instead of leading the project.
items.because: Its stated scope and results would draw attention sooner, if verified as belonging to the food-bank project.
